h2: Tonight, your friends decide what happens next.
p1: When friends hang out, a lot of the night is everyone on their own phone.
p2: Tabletop games fix that. But someone has to run the game, so most groups never play.
p3: So Meta's Muse runs it. The TV is the table, your phones are the controllers, and every story really happened.
d1: Scan the code. No app, no account. Name your character, describe them in one line, and add your secret talent.
d2: Your hero is exactly what you typed, painted in by Muse.
d3: Muse turns a real, odd news story into tonight's adventure.
d4: On your turn, you tell the table your plan, and your friends pitch ideas from their phones.
d5: Use one, and their name goes up on screen.
d6: Every hero has Guts, Brains and Charm: force, tricks and talk.
d7: Swipe up to throw. Code rolls the dice, never the AI.
d8: Muse takes your plan literally, writes what happens next, and paints a new scene.
d9: For the finale, everyone gets thirty seconds to convince each other.
d10: Then you back a plan, and the whole table shakes their phones at once.
r1: And the twist. Here's what you did.
a1: Muse runs the night. Muse Spark picks odd news that makes a good, safe story, judges every plan, and writes every turn.
a2: Muse Image paints your heroes into every scene. Code rolls the dice, and the AI judges ideas, never people.
a3: Every brain in this game is Meta's Muse. The only thing it borrowed is a voice.
t1: It was built by a first-time hacker making every creative call, with Claude Code as lead engineer, running a team of agents.
t2: They watched our playtests frame by frame. Our worst run is why we rebuilt the story around the players' choices.
t3: A test harness plays whole games with real Muse calls, and a better rubric took Muse Spark from five of eight fair rulings to eight.
e1: Play free at groupproject-game dot vercel dot app.
